title: Notating In a Mist with Bix and Jack Robbins's added theme
summary: Publisher Jack Robbins asked him to get Bix's piano piece on paper, which took about six months and ended with Bix improvising an ending and a slow theme.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Like those things that came out later, Bix and His Gang and all those kind of things.

But this is the fall of -- I think it's 27. -- No, '28. And we have a guy, Jack Robbins, who was a great publisher, I think, and he was in business with Paul. They had a thing called Whiteman Publications and he was hanging around the band quite a bit and he wanted -- like he got Malnyck and Signorelli together to do "Stairway to the Stars," or something like that, whatever they could do, write it down, I'll publish it, and of course, he's figuring Whiteman will play it.

Which is all logical, but it's a step in the right direction, to have a guy like Robbins, he put these things out very nicely. He had a great publishing company to do it. So I got -- he stopped in some place to see me or I stopped in

with him and he said, "You know that thing of Bix's, well, he had a guy up in the office there, that got together with Bix and Bix, of course, along with some of his drinking and a couple of other things, didn't always get together with the guy and he had some problems, he couldn't get it down.

So he said, "I tell you what I'd like you to do," he said, "I'd like you to get that thing of Bix's down on paper." Well, I said, "that's all right with me if it's all right with Bix." "Oh, that would be all right," so Bix was of course -- he thought I should have done it in the first place, but you know a guy with his own team up there, he knew what they wanted to do, so anyway, it didn't work out.

So Bix and I, we got together and we got together first in Philadelphia, it was a matter of being a little diplomatic about getting him -- if he wanted to do a little drinking, get him aside and put it down. He was enthusiastic about getting it down, but boy that "IN" a Mist," that thing came along and it was rough. Sometimes we'd just get together and get a couple of bars and then the band was on the road all the time. I wasn't.

But I'll bet it took us about six months to get that thing down. First of all in about the middle of it, we had finished the part that he had done, most of the part that he had made a record an arrangement of. He does those little things of his that are rhythmical and he plays his piano and then at

the end it ran to about two minutes 2, 15 or something like that, so he sits down there and he improvises and plays it, you know the way he goes, he just went over the thing and just faked along for about a half hour, until he got the three minutes, and that was it. That's the record.

So anyway we got it down and Jack comes along one day and says, 'Look, this is fine,' but he says, 'You know how the Rhapsody in Blue is?' He says, 'You get a lot of those fireworks and so forth, and in the middle you get that theme? Da, da (sings) I'd like him to write a slow theme, a major theme and we add it to this and that will be it.'

Well, that hit Bix fine, in no time at all, he came up with the theme that he wanted. But here again, he didn't do anything like cross-hand piano to get it -- (sings) he didn't it down in the other register. He still sticks in this same register and that's what I say is the same thing with Eastwood Lane, pretty much. They play like they're playing a single line instrument, and they're playing it on a certain part of the piano. And that part they didn't develop. They didn't have the orchestral education; they had the feeling.

So -- and Bix had a couple of nice little things and have, nice little things that can be orchestrated, but he still had this one thing -- he really knew he had to use a trumpet, and saxophone, or an oboe, something in that register, and you would have to orchestrate it so that like when I did this, you
will find it's all like in the one -- in the staff or maybe a little bit above, all the way through the melody. I don't know if I'm making myself clear -- I'm doing a good job of clouding this up.
